Accepted by World Development on the 8th of October 2025 MINH TAM BUI , IVO VLAEV AND KATSUSHI IMAI https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2025.1072011 Abstract Ageing societies pose an increasing demand for elderly care, particularly in developing countries where formal long-term care infrastructure remains underdeveloped. In these contexts, unpaid family caregivers, especially women, play a crucial role. However, gender care gaps shaped by prevailing social gender norms are seldom quantified, and the underlying factors behind these gaps remain underexplored in the literature. This paper investigates gender differences in elderly caregiving and examines how social gender norms influence caregiving patterns. Using nationally representative Thai time-use data from 2014-15 and the Labor Force Survey from 2013-15, we address two main questions (i) How does the social gender norm around altruism affect the gender care gap for the elderly, directly or indirectly, and through which channels? and (ii) How do men and women trade off care burdens with paid work or leisure time? We contribute to the body of literature on unpaid care work by analyzing the gender differentials in trade-offs associated with elder caregiving as both main and secondary activities. We develop a novel altruistic time ratio (ATR), defined as the time individuals allocate to others relative to time spent on themselves. We quantify the social gender norm (SGN) as the gender mean difference in ATRs, aggregated at the district-area level. The wide variation of SGN across Thai regions offers a broader societal perspective beyond individual and household characteristics in understanding caregiving behavior. I. Introduction The world’s population is growing older due to increasing life expectancy and falling fertility rates UNDESA (2019). Over the last decades, many developed and developing countries alike have dramatically experienced significant demographic shifts, posing unprecedented challenges to national health and social care systems (Ogawa et al., 2021). Meanwhile, long- term care (LTC) systems rely heavily on informal carers in both advanced and emerging economies (Courtin et al., 2014). Informal (unpaid) caregiving by family members, friends, and communities remains the primary source of LTC for the elderly in both measures, the number of carers and the hours they spend on eldercare (Chari et al., 2015; Courtin et al., 2014). 2 Women represent the majority of family caregivers, and their work is predominantly unpaid. Across 13 countries in the Asia-Pacific, women spend two to ten times more on unpaid care work than men, and when paid and unpaid work are combined, women work longer hours than men each day in all countries except New Zealand (ILO & UNDP, 2018). Around the world, women and girls are performing more than three-quarters of the total unpaid care work (Addati et al., 2018). At the household level, ageing leads to a gradual shift of familial care needs from childcare to elder care. Adults may spend more years caring for their parents than caring for their children, as society is ageing (Bookman & Kimbrel, 2011). Such combined responsibilities of women often lead to restrictions in their labor supply, labor market outcomes, typically low-paid, part-time, precarious jobs (Chari et al., 2015; Charmes, 2019; Coverman, 1983) while also negatively affecting their physical and mental well-being with limited time for leisure (Kossek et al., 2019). Ample empirical evidence across countries demonstrates a gender gap in unpaid care provision, the underlying drivers of these gaps at the micro level remain underexplored. Our study aims to fill that empirical gap in the literature on elderly care in low- and middle- income countries. More specifically, we ask the following research questions: (i) What explains the gender difference in altruistic behavior and, consequently, its effects on eldercare? (ii) Does the social gender norm (SGN)2 on altruism affect the elderly care gap 0F between male and female caregivers? (iii) How can the care burdens be traded off with the men’s/women’s paid work or leisure time? (iv) Does the social gender norm influence elderly care time directly or indirectly, and through which channels? 2 We define the social gender norm (SGN) on altruism as the difference between the average of individual altruistic time ratios for women and men at the district-area level. This will be discussed in Section III. 3 Thailand has experienced a rapid increase in the elderly population. Over 30 years, 1994- 2024, the share of elder people aged over 60 years doubled to 14.9% of the population in 2014 and then continued to rise even faster recently, reaching 20% in 2024 (equivalent to 14 million people), according to the surveys on older persons by the National Statistical Office (NSO, 2017, 2024). Officially being a complete aged society poses an urgent need for eldercare provision in the economy and society. Although most of the elders in Thailand (99.2%) receive medical treatment benefits from universal health insurance and other forms, daily care is essential in terms of physical health as well as mental well-being (NSO, 2017). Ample anecdotal evidence has been documented on the essential role of familial care in favor of so-far limited formal or institutional care in Thailand (Ayudhya et al., 2007; Knodel et al., 2013; Knodel et al., 2018; TGRI, 2017). The prevalent preference for family members, especially adult children, over nonrelatives to be caregivers for elderly people and the dominant tradition of relying on adult children in providing care have caused challenges for long-term care alternatives for the public and private sectors (Knodel et al., 2013). More than being altruistic, in an Asian culture like in Thailand, caring for elderly parents as being katanyu (in Thai) has been rooted in social, cognitive, physical, environmental, and economic factors (Ayudhya, et al., 2007). Katanyu is a duty of repayment or an act of reciprocity. Katanyu, rooted in Buddhist values, reflects a socially ascribed sense of obligation for adult children to express gratitude to their parents for raising them by caring for them in their old age (Netiparatanakul, 2020). 4 The present study draws on the latest nationally representative time-use survey3 of 1F Thailand from 2014/2015-an invaluable data source rarely available in low- and middle- income countries. To our knowledge, this is the first study in Thailand to measure elderly care using highly accurate time-use records. Previous research on ageing in Thailand has typically relied on surveys of older persons or small-scale qualitative data. A key conceptual contribution of our study is the construction of the district-area level indicators on SGNs, enabling us to highlight their regional and rural-urban variations across Thailand. Given its strong cultural foundations in filial piety, reciprocity and parental care, Thailand offers a particularly compelling case for examining elderly care within the context of gender and social expectations. Our paper makes the following contributions to the empirical literature on ageing in low- and middle-income countries. First, we quantify altruistic behavior to construct the social gender norm on altruism at the district-area level and thus bring new empirical insights into how broader societal norms shape gendered caregiving patterns apart from conventional factors of individual and household characteristics. This strand of literature is often studied by sociologists and demographers in a contextual approach that allows understanding of gender at a broader societal level beyond individual characteristics (Riley, 1999). Second, with the detailed analysis of eldercare time as primary or secondary activities of caregivers, we can draw some insightful implications of how men and women are (un)willing to trade off their paid work (or leisure time) to accommodate caregiving responsibilities. To our knowledge, this unique feature makes our paper stand out from existing studies on time-use 3 The data are nationally representative at the household level and for care providers but not adequate to assume representativeness of the elderly population as discussed in section III. 5 data, focusing only on main tasks while ignoring supervisory care and multitasking. Finally, we dive deeper into the influence of SGN on the gender care gap by decomposing its direct and indirect effects (through other time uses and their substitution effects) and thereby suggesting suitable policy and/or behavioral interventions. Our findings based on the single and multi-equation Tobit models for both elderly carers and non-carers indicate that (i) the social gender norm increases elderly care time for women and decreases it for men, and (ii) significant tradeoffs exist between elderly care time, leisure time, and paid work. The results show that SGN also indirectly increases elderly care time for women by significantly reducing leisure time and paid work time, although with a smaller magnitude. Literature on Elderly Care and Social Gender Norms Care is defined as the activity that provides what is necessary for the health, well-being, maintenance, and protection of someone. Care is the creation, development, and maintenance of human capabilities and the quality of life from birth to death (Folbre, 1986). Unpaid care work refers to all unpaid services provided within a household for its members, including care, housework, and voluntary community work (Elson, 2002). The activity involves mental or physical efforts and is costly in terms of time resources. Motivation for Familial Eldercare Two main relevant strands of scholarship are highlighted to understand the motivation of family members providing care for their older ones, namely: (i) the economics of unpaid care work and its division within households and (ii) sociological models of intrinsic motives for care provision. The idea of ‘for love or for money’ (Folbre & Nelson, 2000) and the concept of unconditional versus conditional giving (Kohli & Künemund, 2003) provide a common understanding that intergenerational transfers and caring comprise several motivations. The assistance that adult children often provide to their elderly parents may combine prosocial and extrinsic motivations (England et al., 2012). Unconditional motives emphasize altruism, reciprocity, and normative obligation, while conditional motives are more associated with direct exchange (Kohli & Künemund, 2003). Care and assistance can be motivated by both altruistic concerns for the parent’s well-being and an internalized sense of reciprocal obligations or may result from extrinsic rewards, such as direct expectations of payback or bequest from parents or wages and other benefits from market work (with opposite effects) following the framework in Ryan and Deci (2020). Theoretically, in economics, the costs of caregiving are often discussed as a loss of time that could be spent on leisure or paid work. Economic analysis on the motivations of care 7 work has focused more on quantitative aspects such as the forgone income, time costs on care or even the low-paid formal care work (i.e., the external rewards). Still, it often understates the significant nature of care in terms of intrinsic motivations and personal attachment (England et al., 2012). Unlike other goods, motivations for care provision go beyond the extrinsic rewards emphasized by economists (wages, benefits, expected bequests) or even sociologists (social approval or penalties) to include prosocial motivations with intrinsic rewards, such as gratification to help or a desire to make care recipients better off (England et al., 2012). Hence, the simple contrast between doing something for love and doing something for money is not necessarily exclusive in familial care work. Instead, they can be combined in enormous variations (Folbre & Nelson, 2000). Meanwhile, sociological models also theorize motivations for interactions within the family through five primary motivations, including (1) altruism, (2) exchange/reciprocity, (3) trust and common preferences, (4) biological predispositions and (5) social/cultural norms (Bianchi & Joseph McGarry, 2007). In particular, the notions of altruism and reciprocity to motivate intergenerational relationships can also arise from and are maintained by social and cultural norms. Similar conclusions were found in sociological research, which shows that motivation for giving and caring to kin consists of a complex pattern with a high degree of interactions among different motives (Kohli & Künemund, 2003). Intrinsic motivation plays a vital role in care work, and prosocial motivation is central to the provision of high-quality care (England et al., 2012). Altruistic behaviors, stemming from many motives, are important for family caregiving. Most countries in the Asia-Pacific region still rely on families to support older people in terms of financial assistance and care. Altruism and filial piety toward parents remain core values and cultural norms in society underlying intergenerational relations in many Eastern and Southern Asian societies. Adult children in Eastern Asia typically hold strong beliefs and 8 social norms regarding respect and obligations to assist their parents, sacrificing for parents, co-residing and taking care of parents in return for the parental generation’s devotions (Knodel et al., 2018). The Role of Social Norms In psychological literature, social connectedness is the degree to which people or groups have relationships that create a sense of belonging and being cared for, valued, and supported. Social connectedness can facilitate the creation and impact of social norms, which are the unwritten rules of beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors that are considered acceptable in a particular social group or culture (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005). Therefore, humans are strongly influenced by what others do (Cialdini, 2007). Norms have a stronger impact if the target audience is closely related to the group doing the desired behavior (i.e., ‘people like you’), which means strong peer effects on behavior (Schultz et al., 2007). In other words, peer effects on caring responsibilities can emerge because social connectedness can increase the exposure and awareness of social norms among people who share similar experiences, culture, and common pursuits, which can also enhance the feeling of belonging to one’s family or other people with shared identities (Bayer et al., 2016). Peer effects also emerge because social connectedness can foster the development and maintenance of social norms by providing feedback and reinforcement for conforming or deviating from the expected behaviors (i.e., people who are socially connected are more likely to receive approval or disapproval from others based on their adherence to social norms). Concerning normative obligations, the literature on gender inequality and social gender norms has been discussed at the center of unpaid care work and the care economy in general. Theoretically, gender norms and gender wage gaps interplay at the household level and the economy at large in determining the extent of long-term care that men and women provide to 9 their elder family members (Barigozzi et al., 2020; González et al., 2022). Social gender norms refer to the informal rules and the cultural and societal expectations that dictate how men and women are supposed to behave in altruistic or caregiving roles (West & Zimmerman, 1987). These norms are socially constructed and reinforced through institutions like family, education, and religion (Ridgeway, 2011). In the context of altruism, gender norms can influence how men and women engage in unpaid care work, with women often expected to take on more nurturing roles. Similarly, some sociologists emphasize the social construction of norms and values, examining the ways they may be shaped by institutional arrangements of familial caring (Bianchi & Joseph McGarry, 2007). Empirically, the role of women, particularly daughters, as primary caregivers for parents is well-documented from the early literature of social work that daughters are more likely than sons to provide care to an impaired parent (Dwyer & Coward, 1991; Pratt et al., 1989). Historically, women have been the primary and often only caregivers, while the role of sons as primary elder caregivers drew much later attention (Coward & Dwyer, 1990; Dwyer & Coward, 1991). Elderly care is also dependent on the network of siblings, where daughters from mixed-gender networks reported significantly higher levels of stress and burden and more hours spent on caregiving than sons in the US (Checkovich & Stern, 2002; Grigoryeva, 2017). In the same line, Riley (2013) discusses the importance of understanding influences at the larger societal level, beyond the effects of individual and household characteristics, and illustrates how women use their urban status to renegotiate power dynamics within rural families. On the contrary, Abril et al. (2015) show that gender norms and institutional constraints influence women’s predisposition to adjust their preferences regarding work and childcare. 10 The Tradeoffs between Care and Other Activities Time allocation choices within a day for any individual among paid work, unpaid work and leisure, as well as the division of such work among family members (men and women), are determined by various individual, household demographic characteristics and societal and economic factors. While the traditional microeconomic theory of labor underscores the substitutability of paid work and leisure in the neoclassical framework to understand labor supply, the seminal work of Becker (1965) gave a foundation for the “new home economics” with time allocation playing a central role in the household production model, acknowledging the role of home production which is neither paid work or leisure. Although Becker did not explicitly mention the model’s applicability to care as an example of household production, the division of labor in household production in his model is based on comparative advantage by which women should specialize in home production because they are good at homemaking, caring and nurturing and thus their best option, implying that men are better placed to be engaged in market paid work. Folbre (1986) criticizes the unitary household model in which the household is treated as “almost a wholly, cooperative, altruistic unit”, whereas Chiappori & Lewbel (2015) extend Becker’s model to the collective household model to address some of Folbre’s criticisms. The tradeoff between caring and earnings is highly gendered (Bookman & Kimbrel, 2011) because women who care for the elderly tend to reduce their work hours, leave the workforce, or make other adjustments that have unfavorable financial or career implications. The well-known economic literature on the relationship between informal care responsibilities and labor market participation often discusses the issue of “chicken and egg” due to their endogeneity (Heitmueller, 2007). Caring responsibilities are also related to the quality of female employment, with the unequal amount of time spent by women on unpaid care work increasing the probability that 11 they will be engaged in part-time or vulnerable employment (Hegewisch & Gornick, 2011). Moreover, care responsibilities also negatively affect caregivers’ physical and mental well- being, leaving them with limited time for leisure (Kossek et al., 2019). Using the American time use data (ATUS) Kimmel & Connelly (2007) also modelled four time uses, including childcare, home production, market work and leisure to measure their tradeoffs. Among different factors, wage is probably one of the most important factors that determine people’s choice of time allocation between paid and unpaid work. The Context of Elder Care in Thailand Thailand has become an ageing society with a rapid increase in the elderly population and a decline in fertility rates (Peek et al., 2016). At the macro level, the age dependency ratio rebounded from the trough in 2010 (39%) to 42% in 2020 (World Bank, 2021). Low fertility and high longevity mean a switch of the dependency ratio from the young (0-14 years) to the old (60 years and over), causing an increasing burden on the economy by the elderly population (from a share of 9% in 2002 to 18% in 2020). Equivalently, at the household level, familial care needs have gradually shifted from childcare to elder care as in high- income countries (Bookman & Kimbrel, 2011). However, in high-income countries, adult children may not anticipate providing personal care services to their elderly parents and may not face a legal requirement to do so (Kohli & Künemund, 2003). The opposite can be seen in Asian culture. With an underdeveloped institutional long-term care (LTC) in low and middle- income countries in Asia, formal LTC systems remain in a nascent stage and LTC for the elderly is primarily provided by family members, who are informally employed women and sometimes the elderly themselves (World Bank, 2016). Therefore, people still rely on families to support the elderly in terms of financial assistance and care. Adult children in Eastern Asia typically hold strong beliefs regarding respect and obligations to assist their 12 parents (Kim et al., 2015), sacrificing for parents, co-residing and taking care of parents in return for the parental generation’s devotion (Knodel et al., 2018). In Thailand, despite the demographic change described above, financial and non-financial support for older parents remains largely intact (Teerawichitchainan, 2020). Gender inequality among caregivers is also an issue in Thailand. Traditional Thai society dictates that women are to care for their homes and families, including both children and ageing relatives (Peek et al., 2016). It is also a deeply entrenched normative acceptance that women (such as daughters and daughters-in-law) are the appropriate gender to provide personal care (Knodel et al., 2018). As for spousal caregiving, women are more likely to be the care providers to their husbands, who are typically older than their wives. There has not been a cultural adaption with men adopting more domestic responsibilities than before, given the changing role of women at home and outside as breadwinners when few families can afford to survive on a single income, especially in urban areas (Peek et al., 2016). Research on Thai ageing relies extensively on the Older Persons Survey dataset of the NSO. To our knowledge, no studies have analyzed elderly care using this detailed Thai time- use survey dataset.4 2F Hypotheses Motivated by the above discussions about the gender bias in eldercare provision driven by economic, sociocultural, and behavioral factors in Thailand, we propose to test the following three empirical hypotheses. 4 A limited number of studies deployed previous rounds of time-use surveys in 2002 and 2009 (Floro & Pichetpongsa, 2010; Pichetpongsa & Floro, 2007; Yokying & Floro, 2020; Yokying et al., 2016), but these studies looked at the overall unpaid work. 13 H1: The social gender norm (SGN) surrounding altruism5, particularly biased against 3F women, contribute to the unequal distribution of elder caregiving between women and men. Definition of the Altruistic Time Ratio (ATR) To capture behavioral altruism embedded in everyday life, we define the Altruistic Time Ratio (ATR) as the proportion of unpaid time spent on others versus oneself using TUS data. Unpaid time spent on others O i Altruistic Time Ratio = = i Unpaid time spent on self S i The subscript i represents each individual i, O stands for the total duration per day an individual spends unpaid time for (or on) “other” people, whereas S stands for unpaid time 16 which she allocates for “self”. Both O and S are the time spent unpaid.9 The ATR is 7F conceptually grounded in behavioral economic research, especially on dictator games as it is analogous to the concept of ‘splitting the pie’ which is used to measure altruistic social preferences. In these games, individuals are given a certain number of resources to allocate between themselves and others (Forsythe et al., 1994). On average, dictators give about 28 percent of the pie (Engel, 2011). In our case, time is a resource, but it offers the same behavioral logic - allocating one’s own time to benefit others without direct payoff. These insights help us interpret the ATR in a broader view of a person's altruistic orientation and a revealed preference for prosocial behavior under real-life time constraints. More detailed discussion of the relevant literature to justify the ratio is provided in Section B of the Online Appendices. The Social Gender Norm on Altruism Although we aim to examine the altruistic motivation behind elderly caregiving, the regression of an individual’s elderly care time on her altruistic time ratio can be empirical concerns. The estimate may be subject to endogeneity bias as elderly care constitutes a component of overall unpaid work dedicated to others. Therefore, the estimated coefficient is likely to be upwardly biased. To mitigate this endogeneity problem, we define the social gender norm on altruism as the difference between the average of individual altruistic time ratios for women and men at the district-area level. A high level of SGN induces women to be more altruistic while allowing men to be less altruistic in terms of time spent on others relative to themselves. A 10% increase in SGN tends to raise the individual ATR by 0.0786 for women - a much larger degree than the respective decrease in ATR for men (by 0.0224). Notably, all coefficients of SGN across the six cases are statistically significant. Although the magnitude of SGN’s effects on elderly care time and ATR are not directly comparable, the gender ratios of marginal effects (in absolute values) reveal a meaningful insight. In Cases 1 and 2, the female-male ratio is less than 1 (0.54), whereas in Cases 5 and 6 it substantially rises to 3.50. This suggests that SGN not only shapes men’s and women’s altruistic behavior in opposite ways but also disproportionately pressures women by encouraging them to be highly altruistic and consequently devote more time to eldercare, while allowing men to be less altruistic and reduce their caregiving time to elder family members. On the determinants of ATR in Cases 5-6, following the definition of SGN in Section III, this analysis sheds light on structural influences behind altruistic behavior. First, an individual belonging to a household with more children (both those under 5 years old and those between 6 and 14 years old) tends to be more altruistic, as suggested by positive marginal effects across genders. However, the effect is greater for women, highlighting the disproportionate importance of child caregiving workload. Similarly, ‘Co-residence’ (i.e., living in a household where at least an older person resides with working-age members) significantly increases ATR, with a greater effect for women. Interestingly, age is significantly and positively associated with the ATR only for women. In urban areas, both women and men tend to be less time-altruistic, as indicated by the negative and statistically 31 significant coefficient of the urban dummy variable (Online Appendix Table 5). This aligns with our descriptive finding that SGN tends to be higher in rural areas. Concluding Remarks and Policy Recommendations Using microdata from the time-use survey in Thailand in 2014/2015 combined with the Labor Force Survey data in 2013-2015, this study aims to address a daunting question of the gender gap in unpaid care work and its root cause from the social gender norms toward wom0en while exploring potential tradeoffs with other time uses to narrow the gap. We found that Thai women tend to do unpaid elder care work more frequently and for a longer duration in a day than men, either as the main or secondary activities (2-2.5 hours). Age, education and rural/urban settings have heterogeneous effects on men’s and women’s caregiving. The proxy for altruism based on time allocation reveals that women are more altruistic than men in all dimensions, which aligns with the existing literature on gender and altruistic behavior (England et al., 2012). Our novel measure of the social gender norm (SGN) on altruism, defined as the gender difference in the average altruistic time ratio at the district-area level, varies across regions of Thailand and is often higher in rural areas. A single-equation Tobit model shows that SGN is a strong determinant for the duration of 37 eldercare, confirming its key role in widening gender gaps in caregiving. It increases eldercare time for women and reduces it for men. This is supported by the literature on the role of daughters taking care of elder parents rather than sons (Barigozzi et al., 2020; Coward & Dwyer, 1990; Crawford et al., 1994; Delgado & Tennstedt, 1997; Dwyer & Coward, 1991; Pratt et al., 1989). If elder care is a default responsibility of families in society, it is also the default obligation of women, daughters, and wives, rather than of men, sons and husbands, within families. Changing these stereotypes and norms is challenging and takes time. In analyzing the gender difference in time reallocation behavior for possible tradeoffs, our multi-equation Tobit model for the elderly care time, leisure time, and paid work time reveals significant substitution effects among the three components of time use. The strongest tradeoffs are found between work time and leisure time, with similar magnitudes across genders. In addition, we discover an interesting heterogeneity in swapping paid work for more care work where women are more flexible regardless of type of care (main or secondary activities), while men rarely trade their paid work for any type of care activities. Our results also suggest that, in addition to the direct effects of SGN on the gender care gap, there is an indirect channel through which SGN can widen this care gap by inducing men to work more in the labor market while reducing women’s paid work time and leisure time, though its magnitude is relatively small. This is a detrimental side effect of SGN toward gender equality in economic opportunities, as discussed in the literature (Barigozzi et al., 2020; Klimaviciute & Pestieau, 2023; Pearse & Connell, 2016). Similarly, our findings also align with the existing literature on the limited and statistically insignificant impact of wages in narrowing the care gap because women's paid work is less responsive to wage changes. To discuss the implications of our research, we associate our findings with the 3R framework of Elson (2017) toward reducing the burden of elder care on women caregivers. The model comprises three interconnected dimensions to address unpaid care work in the 38 development agenda, highlighting state’s role: Recognition (of its essential role), Reduction (of care work), and Redistribution (among sectors or individuals). If the objective is to reduce the family care burden on women and increase their income-generating opportunities in the labor market, strong policy responses to support measures to the healthcare system and informal caregivers are imperative. Long-term care insurance may become necessary in Thailand soon, especially when familial unpaid care becomes uncertain (Cremer et al., 2017). For the redistribution objective, based on various evidence from our analysis on the role of SGN, we recommend practical solutions of behavioral interventions to motivate the redistribution of caregiving. For instance, the “commitment effects”, “give back” or “stand together” messages can be utilized in persuasive campaigns to reverse the norms about what men should do in Thai society and to be more involved in elderly care. Such interventions may lead to changes in filial behaviors, even in cultures and societies with deeply rooted altruism and filial piety (Kohli, 1999). Lastly, for the purpose of recognition, without awareness of the informal care value, unpaid work will be underestimated and never viewed as a type of work in household/social reproduction, thereby building up human capital and labor resources for the economy. This is particularly important for understanding the policy landscape for a rapidly ageing society in Thailand. Time-use survey data activity codes Since 2009, the NSO of Thailand has adopted international standards of the ICATUS 2005 (International Classification of Activities for Time Use Statistics) (NSO, 2017). Time diaries record respondents' activities over a 24-hour period, typically describing activities with time periods, including start time and end time, in 10-minute intervals. The United Nations published the trial ICATUS in 2005, followed by a more official guideline on time-use statistics in 2016 (United Nations, 2016). Therefore, the dataset in this study follows the old classification of 15 major divisions of activities, of which group 7 covers work providing unpaid care services to household members. Our analysis focuses on the second class of this group (712), representing care work for dependent adults. Within this class, there are three categories of care, namely, caring for adults/physical care (07121), caring for adults/emotional support (07122) and accompanying adults to places (07123). In particular, the unpaid care services refer to caregiving provided without remuneration either to household and family members or to other households. It should be noted that although the dataset does not allow us to distinguish elder care from the general adult care due to the lack of information on care recipients (and their age) and the ICATUS 2005 classifying these care activities with the same code, we make a “strong” assumption that this is for elder care in general. Such care could also be for disabled or sick members of the households who are not old. The assumption is based on our data from the national survey on older persons (NSO, 2017), which shows the care recipients’ perspective, receiving personal and health-related care from family members. Our descriptive analysis shows that among care recipients aged 20 years old and above, 41.5 per cent are above 65 years old, 10.2 per cent for the age group 60-64; 10.1 per cent for 55-59 and 8.9 per cent for 50-54, making a cumulative sum of over 70 per cent of recipients aged 50 or above. While those recipients are certainly not the ones who receive care from 633 caregivers in our time-use sample - since only one household member was interviewed per household - the similarity in age distribution across both nationally representative surveys supports our assumption that the majority of adult care is elder care. 48 Online Appendix Table 1: Classification of activities by major division, division, group and class Major Division/Group/Class of Activities 01. First, we require activities to be unpaid and strictly measured beyond the time an individual spends on his/her committed paid work, time for learning, etc. The core 49 idea here is that given a certain amount of time left after committed work/study, how an individual allocates her time on (and for) others versus oneself (without any expectation of money/remuneration) matters. By this definition, this indicator is not specific time spent only on older household members, but reflects an overall attitude toward people in the family, community and society. Second, it is a ratio rather than an amount of time and more importantly, it is independent from how much time people have left after their committed tasks. The two extreme examples we can imagine from this indicator are a very altruistic man/woman who spends most of their available time caring for their children, their elder parents, on cooking, cleaning, laundry or even helping their frail neighbors while spending very minimum time on their sleep, watching TV, let alone playing sports or attending social events, etc. On the other extreme, we have a very selfish (self-interested) man/woman who spends no time on other people around them, but all their free time after work on their interests like sleeping, watching TV and social media, and hobbies. Based on 15 major divisions of activities in ICATUS which is used in Thai time use survey data and on the two key questions asked in the survey, we can calculate the amount of time individuals spend on OTHERS (O) and on ONESELF (S) to come up with the “Altruistic proxy” time ratio. The two key questions are: 1. Is this activity PAID or UNPAID? 2. For whom are you doing this activity? The answer can be one of the following: (1) oneself, (2) own family members, (3) other family members, (4) own and other family members, (5) community. To be counted as “time for others”, an activity in the survey must meet two conditions, namely UNPAID for the 1st question and all options except the first for the 2nd question. Therefore, it covers all activities in the major divisions 6 and 7 in the above table as well as 8 if the community work is unpaid. As for “self-time”, two similar conditions include UNPAID and option 1 for the 2nd question. Certainly, all the major divisions of activities from 10 to 15 fall under “self-time”. However, we also double-check the purpose of each using question 2. Some examples to clarify this definition are when you cook a meal at home only for your consumption but not for other family members, it is counted as “self-time” even though it is unpaid. But if a mother of three spends two hours each day preparing breakfast and dinner for the whole family, it will be considered “time for others” even though she also consumes the meals she makes. 50 As previously mentioned regarding the quality of time spent on others as another aspect of altruistic behavior, we do not have qualitative information from the time use survey to evaluate people’s satisfaction or happiness when receiving or spending time with others. However, we presume that how much attention you dedicate to your activities to some extent reflects your efforts and the level of care. For this, there is information on the main (primary) and secondary tasks, asking respondents, “What are you also doing at the same time when performing this primary activity?”. Multitasking can be seen very often in our daily lives. A typical example of young parents is when they are working at home on their computers, keeping an eye on their toddler playing around the house. This is called supervisory care, and we also count it as “time for others” besides the same amount of time for paid work. Similarly, an individual can also watch TV or listen to music while doing their main activity of cooking or domestic chores. In this case, the time they spend is double counted as “time for others” and “time for oneself”. This concept is considered to produce the second version of the altruistic time measure, which covers both primary and secondary activities. However, given the lack of any attitude questions in the Thai time-use survey, we are trying to measure something non-quantitative in nature but using numerical variables. Therefore, it is certainly far from perfect measure. While we use these ratios for descriptive analysis, they are not directly included in regression equations for eldercare time to avoid potential endogeneity. This altruistic time ratio is conceptually founded in behavioral economics literature, as it is analogous to the concept of ‘splitting the pie’ in dictator games. In these games, individuals are given a certain amount of resources to allocate between themselves and others (Forsythe et al., 1994). In our case, the ratio is calculated in terms of ‘time for others’ versus ‘time for oneself’, whereas in a typical dictator game, it involves the proportion of money allocated to others versus oneself. Here, we conceptualize altruism as a course of action that extends beyond mere motivation, meaning that the way people spend their time reflects altruistic actions. Our measure is conceptually motivated by the literature on dictator games supporting the comparison between “other” and “self” using different types of resources such as money, time and love to model individual preferences for resource distributions for a variety of issues (e.g., political participation, career choices, intergenerational resource allocations, behavioral differences across genders; Couch et al., 1999; Andreoni & Miller, 2002; Eckel, 2008; Dawes et al., 2011; Engel, 2011; Porter and Adams, 2016) activities. The concept of the altruistic time ratio also has a sociological basis, as it reflects broader sociological theories on altruism, social exchange, and time allocation; for example, theories 51 of social exchange explore how individuals invest time and resources in relationships, motivated by altruism and social obligations (Blau, 1964). In social capital theory, time is considered a resource invested in relationships, family, or community, and it can be allocated in ways that reflect social obligations and structures (Bourdieu, 1986). Therefore, we conceptualize altruism as a course of action beyond just motivation, meaning that the way people spend their time indicates altruistic action. There exists some literature supporting the comparison between “other” and “self” using different types of resources such as money, time, and love, as in Couch et al. (1999). For instance, there is evidence in the literature on experimental games where altruism is measured in the lab using dictator games. In a standard dictator game, each subject is assigned a role as either a dictator or a recipient. Dictators are given fixed resources (money or tokens), and they are paid for the amount they decide to keep for themselves, while recipients are paid for the amount the dictators decide to pass. On average, dictators give about 28 percent of the pie (Engel, 2011). The modified dictator games (Andreoni & Miller, 2002) were created to identify heterogeneous distributional preferences among populations. Participants in such studies make multiple allocation decisions by playing a series of dictator games that vary both the relative price of giving and the available budget. Varying the price allows measuring selfishness (allocation to self) while varying the endowment allows measuring efficiency- equality tradeoffs (concerns for increasing total payoffs versus concerns for reducing differences in payoffs between self and others). Therefore, such games measure distributional preferences which have been used to explain issues such as political participation (Dawes et al., 2011), career choices and, more relevant for our study, intergenerational sharing (Porter and Adams, 2016) and gender difference (Eckel, 2008). This literature would justify our altruistic time ratio, which uses the same structure where agents are supposed to distribute time rather than money or tokens. JSON: Name: sgn_eldercare_thailand Title: Quantifying the causal effect of district-level social gender norms on gender differences in unpaid eldercare time using Tobit and multivariate Tobit models Short Hypothesis: An increase in district-level social gender norm (measured as the gender difference in average altruistic time ratios) causes an increase in women's daily eldercare time and a decrease in men's daily eldercare time, thereby widening the gender gap in eldercare minutes per day. Related Work: Prior empirical approaches measure unpaid care with time-use surveys and analyze determinants with OLS or single-equation censored models (Tobit) and occasionally selection models (Heckman). Multivariate approaches (SUR, multivariate Tobit) have been used to model joint time-allocation decisions (paid work, leisure, unpaid care) but typically ignore secondary/multitasked care and contextual social norms. Experimental literature (dictator games) provides micro measures of altruism but is not linked to field-level time-use. Existing macro/contextual work relies on broad regional indicators or household-level norms; it rarely constructs a localized, gender-differenced altruism aggregate (district-level SGN) or quantifies how contextual norms shift both the level and gender distribution of care while allowing for substitution across time uses. Limitations in prior work include omitted treatment of multitasking/supervisory care, limited attention to instrument strength and endogeneity of altruism measures, sparse use of multiequation Tobit estimators for correlated time-use decisions, and weak external validity across subnational heterogeneity. Abstract: This project tests whether localized social gender norms on altruistic behavior causally shape gender differences in unpaid eldercare time. Using Thailand's nationally representative 2014–15 time-use survey merged with 2013–15 labor force data, we (1) construct an individual-level Altruistic Time Ratio (ATR) as unpaid time allocated to others versus self and (2) aggregate ATR by district-area into a Social Gender Norm (SGN) defined as the female-minus-male mean ATR. We estimate single-equation Tobit, Instrumental-Variable Tobit, and multivariate Tobit systems (eldercare, leisure, paid work) to quantify direct and indirect SGN effects and tradeoffs across time uses. Identification exploits district-level SGN variation, peer leisure-mode instruments, and imputed province wages from an out-of-sample wage equation. The main contribution is an integrated empirical pipeline that: (a) operationalizes a time-based altruism metric at individual and contextual levels, (b) models censoring and correlated time-use choices with simulation-based MLE, and (c) decomposes direct versus substitution channels that produce gendered care burdens. Expected outcome: robust estimates of SGN-driven shifts in women's and men's eldercare minutes and quantification of substitution elasticities with paid work and leisure. Experiments: Datasets: (a) Thailand Time-Use Survey (TUS) 2014–15: 73,306 diaried individuals (10-minute intervals); analysis sample: individuals aged >=15 (n≈63,174), caregivers identified (n≈633); (b) Labor Force Survey (LFS) 2013: used to estimate out-of-sample imputed wage by province. Variable construction: ATR_i = unpaid_time_on_others / unpaid_time_on_self (two variants: primary-only and primary+secondary multitask). SGN_k = mean_female(ATR)_k - mean_male(ATR)_k for district-area k (k≈1,558; drop districts with <10 observations in sensitivity checks). Main estimands: average partial effects (APE) of SGN on elderly_care_time (minutes/day) by gender; substitution correlations (rho) between elderly_care, leisure, paid_work from multivariate Tobit; IV-local average treatment effects where leisure or paid_work are endogenous. Models and baselines: (1) OLS and OLS with robust SE clustered at district; (2) single-equation Tobit (primary and primary+secondary definitions); (3) Heckman selection model (probit selection + linear outcome) as alternative; (4) multivariate Tobit (mvtobit) system for three time uses estimated by simulated MLE with GHK replications=100; (5) IV-Tobit where endogenous regressors (leisure or paid_work) instrumented by (a) district-gender-age cohort peer_leisure_mode and (b) imputed province wage; compare with 2SLS on linearized outcomes for diagnostics. Evaluation metrics and tests: APE (minutes/day) with robust cluster SE, p-values; likelihood-ratio test for joint significance of rho matrix; first-stage F-statistic for instrument strength; Hansen J (overidentification); bootstrapped 95% CIs for APEs; predicted vs observed RMSE for fitted conditional expectation of time-use (using Tobit-predicted e(0,.)); sensitivity metrics: change in gender gap minutes attributable to direct SGN effect and indirect substitution channels. Ablations and robustness checks (minimum one required): (A) remove secondary activities (primary-only vs primary+secondary), (B) alternate SGN aggregation levels (province, municipality), (C) drop districts with sample size cutoffs at 5, 10, 20, (D) omit peer_leisure instrument and re-run IV and first-stage diagnostics, (E) propensity-score matched sample of carers vs non-carers to test selection robustness, (F) alternative ATR definitions (exclude community unpaid work, exclude household production), (G) estimate models separately by urban/rural and by age-cohort to test heterogeneity. Reporting: report APEs by gender, rho estimates with z-statistics, first-stage F>10 requirement, Hansen J p-values, LR test p-values, and bootstrapped CIs for all main contrasts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error: ATR and SGN depend on time-use coding and the assumption that adult-care codes predominantly reflect eldercare; misclassification biases APEs. Endogeneity: SGN may correlate with unobserved district-level confounders (culture, LTC availability); instruments (peer leisure mode, imputed wage) risk weak identification or violate exclusion. Sample size and aggregation: many small district-areas have few observations; SGN estimates in small areas are noisy and can induce attenuation bias. Selection/truncation: Tobit assumes normality and exogeneity of censoring; Heckman requires valid exclusion restrictions which may be unavailable. Multitasking double-counting: inclusion of secondary activities may inflate correlation across time uses and complicate interpretation of substitution elasticities. Computational constraints: multivariate Tobit with large n and many covariates requires simulated MLE (GHK) and may not converge or may produce imprecise estimates with limited replications. External validity: results pertain to Thailand 2014–15 and may not generalize to countries with different LTC systems or cultural contexts. Unobserved recipient characteristics: absent data on care recipients (age, health) limits causal attribution specifically to eldercare. Statistical power: low prevalence of caregivers (n≈633) limits precision for subgroup analysis and IV inference.
